# ALTEN SA (ATE.PA) — Forensic Dossier

*Engineering & Technology Consulting (ESO) / IT services · Euronext Paris · price ~€63 (scan snapshot €57.6) · FY ends Dec 31*

**Source note:** No FMP transcript was bundled. This dossier is built from the live Q1-2026 earnings call (held ~mid-May 2026, via Investing.com transcript), the FY2025 annual results (released ~late Feb / early Mar 2026), the 2026 AGM / dividend notice, and the screener's financial trajectory block. The peer set (Sopra Steria, CGI, CTSH, EPAM, Globant, Capgemini, Akkodis/Adecco) is used as the relative lens. ALTEN is a single-business engineering R&D outsourcer, not a conglomerate — there is no segment-revenue block, so the SoP is whole-company intrinsic, framed by end-market and geographic mix.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

ALTEN's story has inverted over five years. The 2021–2022 narrative was a **post-COVID super-cycle**: revenue ran from €2.93B (2021) to €3.78B (2022, +29%) with net income exploding to €458M and EPS €13.21 — a once-in-a-decade demand snap-back as automotive, aerospace and tech R&D budgets all reopened at once, plus a low tax/one-off-flattered base. Management's tone then was offensive: hiring tens of thousands of engineers, "we cannot recruit fast enough," international expansion.

By 2023–2024 the narrative quietly shifted to **normalization**: revenue plateaued (€4.07B → €4.14B), but net income collapsed from the €458M peak to €233M (2023) then €186M (2024) as the gross/utilization tailwind reversed. The 2022 EPS of €13.21 was never a run-rate — it was a peak-margin print, and management never re-anchored investors off it.

By **FY2025 the narrative is overtly defensive**: revenue actually *fell* to €4,099M (-1.1% reported, **organic -4.5%**), net income more than halved again to €106.9M (-42.6% YoY), and the entire investor message pivoted to **"margin resilience and cash generation in a soft cycle"** — op margin on activity held at ~8.5% "thanks largely to reduced SG&A and good project management," FCF €239.9M, four self-financed acquisitions, net cash. The growth drivers that were emphasized in 2021–22 (automotive R&D, telecoms, semis) are the exact ones now in retreat; the drivers being *introduced* are aerospace, defense/security, energy/nuclear and rail.

In **Q1-2026** the arc continues: headline revenue €1.7B (-0.8% reported) but management's framing leads with **"we have managed to come back to an increasing organic turnover by 1.6%"** at constant perimeter — i.e. the story is now "the FX/perimeter headline understates an organic inflection." H1-2026 organic is guided to **0% to -0.5%**, so even the bull framing concedes the first half is flat-to-down; the recovery is back-half and 2027.

**Net arc:** from "structural compounder riding an engineering super-cycle" → "quality cyclical defending margin and cash through a multi-sector R&D-budget recession, waiting on aerospace/defense/nuclear to pull it out."

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

The inflection is marginal, not a trend break. |

**Synthesis:** the *cash* claims are corroborated; the *organic-inflection* and *margin-resilience* claims are real but heavily framed and not yet visible in the bottom line, which is at a 5-year low. The narrative is modestly richer than the trajectory justifies on growth, and honestly poorer than the 2022 peak that some bulls still anchor to.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: DECLINING (offensive → defensive), with a tentative Q1-26 stabilization.**

- 2021–2022 (inferred from trajectory): offensive — record hiring, double-digit growth, expansion. Confidence high.
- FY2025 call: defensive — the message is cost discipline, cash, "visibility remains uncertain." Language shifted to efficiency and balance-sheet quality.
- Q1-2026: **cautiously stabilizing but hedged.** Management leads with the +1.6% organic positive, but the dominant texture is uncertainty: *"It is extremely difficult to have a forecast,"* *"Macroeconomic, geopolitical context is of a high uncertainty,"* and on semis *"It is a real topic that has to be discussed."* On margin they refuse to commit a number — *"The increase of margin is going to happen by and by."* That is the language of a team that wants to signal a bottom without being held to a timeline.

The shift from "we can't hire fast enough" (2022) to "the increase of margin is going to happen by and by" (2026) is the single clearest tone tell: from demand-constrained growth to cost-managed defense.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: MEDIUM.**

ALTEN has historically been a sandbagger-ish, conservative French mid-cap that under-promises on margin and delivers cash — and FY2025 *did* deliver the cash (€239.9M FCF, dividend maintained at €1.50, net cash). On that axis credibility is intact. But on the **trajectory** they have repeatedly framed each soft year as near a bottom while net income kept halving (458 → 233 → 186 → 107). The screener notes **beat 1/2 quarters (50%)** and **EPS -43.2% YoY** — a coin-flip beat rate against a collapsing base is not a strong delivery record. They are now explicitly declining to give a hard margin target ("by and by") and have guided H1-26 organic to a soft 0% to -0.5%, which is appropriately humble. Management is credible on *cash and balance sheet*, weak-to-unproven on *the timing of the earnings recovery*.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Automotive and Germany.** Auto is 13% of group and German auto R&D is described as **down ~30%**; analysts press on when this stops bleeding. Management has no firm answer — "extremely difficult to forecast."
- **Semiconductors / offshore shift.** Semis -8% and management flags a structural question about **work shifting offshore** ("a real topic that has to be discussed") — analysts are probing whether this is cyclical or a permanent bill-rate/onshore-demand erosion. Management does not resolve it.
- **Margin cadence.** Analysts want a dated margin path; management deflects to "by and by," the classic non-answer.
- **Telecoms -18%.** A "very strong decrease" that gets acknowledged but not given a recovery timeline.
- **AI / automation of engineering hours.** The elephant not fully addressed: ALTEN bills engineering labor-hours at a spread; analysts increasingly ask whether gen-AI compresses billable R&D hours. Management's answer is mix-shift to "complex" work, not a refutation.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Net income down 5 straight halvings of the peak** — €458M (2022) → €107M (2025), EPS €13.21 → €3.03; a -38.8% 3-yr EPS CAGR. The earnings base is genuinely shrinking, not just pausing.
🔴 **Gross margin only ~8.3% and contracting** (screener) — confirms a low-value-add, body-shop-heavy delivery mix relative to true-IP peers; little pricing power.
🔴 **Demand weakness is broad, not isolated** — auto -2.6%, semis -8%, telecoms -18%, life sciences down, Germany/Nordics/Eastern Europe/North America all negative. This is a multi-vertical R&D-budget recession, not one bad segment.
🔴 **Latest-quarter EPS YoY -81%** (scan) and Piotroski only 4/9 — fundamental momentum is poor.
🔴 **Offshore/AI structural question on semis & engineering hours left unresolved** — terminal-value tell for a labor-arbitrage model.

🟢 **Genuine net cash (~€59M; cash €348M > debt €289M)** and **FCF €239.9M** — a real fortress balance sheet and a real SoP add-back; this is not a distressed name.
🟢 **Organic returned to +1.6% (constant perimeter) in Q1-26** — the first positive organic in over a year; a tentative bottoming signal.
🟢 **Aerospace +2%, defense/security +10%, energy/nuclear +10%, rail back to growth** — the European defense + nuclear capex cycle is a real, multi-year tailwind ALTEN is genuinely exposed to.
🟢 **Self-funded M&A engine** (Itsclinic + "2 deals practically finished, 5 underway, 10 in the wings") — disciplined, accretive, no leverage.
🟢 **Founder-led, conservative governance; dividend maintained at €1.50** despite the earnings trough.
🟢 **ROIC 10.6% / ROE 12.8%** — still above cost of capital even at the trough; this is a quality cyclical, not a value trap balance sheet.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **"By and by" margin language** is a deliberate hedge — they believe margin recovers but won't be pinned to a quarter, consistent with a team that has been early on calling the bottom before.
- **Vertical rotation in the commentary** — aerospace/defense/nuclear/rail now lead the script; automotive/telecoms/semis have moved from headline drivers to problem children. This is the same playbook as the broader European ESO cohort (Akkodis/Adecco, Alteia) rotating toward defense.
- **FX is now a recurring villain** — the international book (65% of revenue) is being dinged by a stronger euro; management is leaning on this to explain the reported-vs-organic gap, which is legitimate but also convenient.
- **The "offshore is a real topic" admission** on semis is the most important unguarded line — it concedes that part of the demand softness may be permanent relocation of work, not a cycle.
- **Dividend held flat, not raised** — signals management itself sees this as a trough year, not a base to grow off yet.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE → mildly DETERIORATING on earnings, STABLE on capital allocation.** ALTEN is not deteriorating financially — it is a net-cash, cash-generative, disciplined-M&A operator with a maintained dividend. But the *earnings power* has structurally stepped down (NI €458M → €107M) and the recovery is unproven and back-half-loaded.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing:** *Is the 2025 earnings trough cyclical (R&D budgets reopen as the aerospace/defense/nuclear cycle scales, and ALTEN re-rates off a €107M base toward €200M+) or is part of it a structural bill-rate/hour erosion from offshoring + gen-AI automation of engineering hours?* The valuation (P/FCF ~6x, net cash, DCF/EPV MoS positive) prices in the bear case; the question is purely whether the earnings base is melting or merely depressed.

**Economic moat:** **NARROW.** Moat type = a blend of **switching-cost / intangible-relationship** (embedded multi-year engineering teams inside Airbus/Stellantis/Thales-type clients, security clearances for defense work, domain expertise) plus **scale-cost** (largest pure-play European ESO, ~52k engineers). But the **8.3% gross margin and ROIC stepping down from peak to ~10.6%** show this is a *narrow* moat with limited pricing power — it is a high-quality labor-arbitrage business, not an IP monopoly. ROIC still > WACC, so the moat is real but thin.

**Moat trend:** **ERODING (mildly).** Gross margin is contracting, ROIC and net margin have fallen materially from the 2022 peak, and the semis-offshoring admission points to bill-rate pressure. It is not collapsing (still cash-generative, still positive organic), but the direction is down, not up.

**Secular threat:** **MATERIAL (not yet terminal).** ALTEN sits squarely in the **AI-automation-of-engineering/IT-services-labor-arbitrage** tail: its economics are billing R&D/engineering labor-hours at a spread, exactly the model gen-AI threatens to deflate (book-to-bill pressure, hour decoupling, offshoring). However — unlike a pure code body-shop — a large slice of ALTEN's work is **regulated, safety-critical, security-cleared engineering** (aerospace certification, nuclear, defense) that is far harder to automate or offshore, which is why the threat is *material* rather than *terminal*, and why the defense/nuclear rotation matters as a structural hedge.

**Cheapness verdict:** **mostly a fear-print over a partially-earned discount.** P/FCF ~6x on a net-cash, FCF €240M, ROIC>WACC business that has merely cycled down is cheap; but the ~8% gross margin and the live offshoring/AI question mean the discount to higher-quality peers (CTSH 34% GM, EPAM/GLOB ~27–35% GM) is *partly justified*, not pure mispricing. This is cheap-but-deservedly-cheaper, with a real cyclical recovery option and a real (manageable) secular tail.

A return on capital that is decent but *falling*, with margins compressing, is a narrow moat under pressure, not a wide one.

**Moat trend: ERODING.** Margin on activity has fallen from roughly 10%+ to about 8.5%, and net income has more than halved over two years. Whether that reverses with the cycle is the whole debate.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL (not yet terminal).** The structural risk is labour-arbitrage deflation — artificial-intelligence tools that automate engineering and software tasks, decoupling client value from the billable headcount Alten rents out. Aerospace, defence and regulated R&D are the most defensible niches (safety-critical, certified, relationship-heavy), which is why this is "material" rather than "terminal." But the silence on AI and the eroding margin mean the cheapness is part fear-print, part early warning. A low multiple on a base that may be structurally (not just cyclically) shrinking is the value-trap risk a director must price.

Roughly 51,000 engineers across 35-plus countries. No bundled transcript was supplied; this dossier is built from the company's published 2025 annual results (February 2026), its first-quarter 2026 activity release and call, management's investor presentation, and the screener's financial trajectory.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story has flipped from "structural compounder" to "cyclical trough, awaiting a turn." For most of the last decade Alten told a simple, credible growth story: a global engineering-services champion compounding revenue at double digits through organic hiring plus steady bolt-on acquisitions, with operating margins on activity (the company's preferred profit measure — operating profit before share-based pay and one-offs, as a share of sales) parked around 10%. Since then the narrative has narrowed sharply. By the 2025 annual results the message was defensive: revenue of €4.10B was down 1.1% as reported and down 4.5% on an organic basis (stripping out acquisitions and currency), margin on activity slipped to about 8.5%, and net income collapsed to €107M. Management reframed the year as a cyclical air-pocket concentrated in a few end-markets — German automotive engineering, telecom and semiconductors — rather than a loss of competitive position, pointing to France, Iberia and Italy holding up as proof the franchise is intact.

The most recent communication, the first quarter of 2026, is a "trend-reversal-in-progress" narrative. Management now leads with aerospace and defence reaccelerating (defence up almost 10% year on year), banking and finance turning positive, and a stated hope that the worst end-markets stabilise by year-end. The driver quietly dropped is organic hiring momentum; the driver newly emphasised is acquisitions — a just-signed €60M-revenue, 470-consultant data/cloud deal plus "more than 5 deals underway." The engine has shifted from organic engineering growth to a wait-for-the-cycle-and-buy-the-dip posture.

year), so the "management's words" layer is built from the company's own FY2025 results

2026), and management commentary reported around both — all cross-checked against the hard
financials from our data provider. Where a claim rests only on management's framing rather
than an audited number, it is flagged as such.*

in Europe — an "engineering services" business that rents out roughly 50,000 engineers to
design and test products for carmakers, aerospace and defence primes, rail, energy, life
sciences, telecoms and banks. It is not a diversified IT-services generalist; its economics
swing on the external R&D budgets of a handful of hardware industries, above all automotive

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

was a boom.** Revenue leapt from €2.33 billion in 2020 to €3.78 billion in 2022 (+62% over
two years) as post-pandemic R&D budgets snapped back and Alten bolted on acquisitions;
reported earnings per share spiked to €13.21 in 2022, flattered by a one-off tax benefit.
Management's language in that window was pure offence — headcount growth, new-country
expansion, "structural" demand for outsourced engineering.

**Chapter two (2023–2025) was a plateau that turned into a squeeze.** Revenue stalled in a
narrow €4.07–4.14 billion band for three straight years, and by 2025 it actually shrank —
down 1.1% as reported and down 4.5% on an organic basis (stripping out acquisitions and
currency). The margin story quietly deflated in parallel: the operating margin on ordinary
activity, which had run near 11–12% at the 2022 peak, fell to 8.5% in 2025. Reported net
income collapsed from €233 million in 2023 to €107 million in 2025, and diluted earnings per
share fell from €6.74 to €3.03. The growth drivers management had emphasised — automotive and
German industrial R&D — became the drag, and the narrative shifted defensively to "utilisation
discipline", "cost control" and "limited visibility".

**Chapter three (late 2025 into 2026) is a tentative turn.** In the FY2025 release management
flagged that the slowdown *decelerated* in the fourth quarter, with civil aeronautics and
banking returning to growth and energy and defence accelerating. The Q1 2026 revenue print
then showed organic growth swing back to +1.6% (the reported figure was −0.8%, dragged down by
a weaker dollar and acquisition-integration noise). Management's framing is now cautiously
constructive — "stabilisation and growth" for 2026, a stated ambition to rebuild the operating
margin back toward 10% and grow past 70,000 engineers over time — but they are candid that
"visibility remains limited" and that the first half of 2026 is the test of whether the
recovery is real. The arc, in short: boom, to squeeze, to an unconfirmed inflection.

depressed 2025 net income), but on cash flow it is strikingly cheap** (enterprise value —
market value plus debt minus cash — of about 4.4 times earnings before interest, tax,
depreciation and amortisation, and 5.6 times free cash flow, with net cash on the balance
sheet). The gap between the two is the whole debate: is 2025 a cyclical trough of a
cash-generative franchise, or the first leg down of a structurally shrinking base?

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: turning (from declining).** Through 2023–2025 the tone shifted unmistakably from
offensive to defensive — from "structural growth" and expansion to "utilisation", "cost
discipline" and "reduced visibility", matching a business whose organic revenue was sliding.
The FY2025 and Q1 2026 communications mark the first genuine change in that register: management
volunteered that the deceleration is easing and that specific end-markets (civil aerospace,
banking, energy, defence) have turned up, while being careful *not* to over-promise — they
explicitly withheld precise 2026 margin guidance and called out that the first half is the
proof point. That combination — more constructive but deliberately unguided — reads as honest
rather than promotional.

**Reliability: Medium-to-High.** The single cleanest test available — management "anticipated"
roughly an 8.1% operating margin for 2025 and delivered 8.5% — was a modest beat, not a miss.

is the hardest thing to fake. Against that, the multi-year record is one of a business that
serially disappointed on *growth* as the automotive/German R&D cycle rolled over, so the
market has learned to discount the "return to 10% margin, 70,000 engineers" ambition until it
shows up in the printed numbers. There is no evidence of sandbagging or of aggressive
accounting; the credibility gap is about cyclical forecasting, not integrity.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The recurring pressure points, evident in how management frames each release, are: (1) **the
depth and duration of the automotive/German weakness** — the one region and end-market
management keeps having to explain away; (2) **whether generative AI structurally deflates
engineering bill-rates and headcount** — the question hanging over every engineering- and
IT-services name in Europe, which management addresses only obliquely (positioning AI as a
productivity tool and a new service line rather than a threat to the labour-hours business
model); and (3) **margin trajectory** — management's refusal to put a dated number on the
10% ambition is exactly the point analysts push on, because the margin is the swing factor
between the cheap-cash-flow bull case and the value-trap bear case.

🔴 Organic revenue turned negative in 2025 (−4.5%), the first real contraction outside a
recession, driven by the automotive and German industrial R&D pullback.
🔴 Return on invested capital has fallen to roughly 6.6% on a trailing basis — below a
reasonable cost of capital — meaning that *at the trough* the business is not currently earning
its keep; whether that reverts is the entire thesis.
🔴 Operating margin has declined three years running (from ~11–12% to 8.5%).
🔴 Goodwill of about €1.24 billion sits on the balance sheet (down from €1.39 billion), a
legacy of the acquisition-led growth era and a future impairment risk if the downturn deepens.
🟢 Net cash balance sheet (cash €348m against €67m of financial debt excluding leases) and a
~17% free-cash-flow yield — genuine downside protection and optionality.
🟢 Q1 2026 organic growth back to +1.6%, with civil aerospace, defence, energy and banking
inflecting up — the first datapoint consistent with a cyclical trough.
🟢 Management delivered slightly above its own margin bar in 2025 and communicates candidly.
🟢 Founder-owner (Azoulay, ~57%) with heavy personal stake aligned to long-run value.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

Two subtle shifts matter. First, **the end-market mix is rotating under the surface**: aerospace,
defence and energy (structurally supported by rearmament and the energy transition) are taking
share of Alten's book from automotive (structurally pressured). That improves the *quality* of
the revenue base even while the headline stalls, and it is why the organic figure inflected
before the automotive market did. Second, **the founder-control structure is the defining
governance fact and it cuts both ways** — it aligns the controlling shareholder with long-term
value and has kept the balance sheet conservative, but it also means an outside activist cannot
force a buyback, break-up or sale, and a takeover is effectively off the table. Any re-rating
here has to come from operational recovery, not from corporate action. The CEO title has passed
from Azoulay to Cyril Malarge, a normal succession rather than a strategic pivot.

**Classification: PIVOTING (turning).** Alten is a high-quality, cash-generative, net-cash
engineering franchise that has just been through a genuine cyclical squeeze in its two biggest
end-markets and is showing the first tentative signs of troughing. Capital allocation is
conservative and shareholder-aligned (steady dividend, bolt-on acquisitions, no financial
leverage), if unexciting — there is no large buyback and, given founder control, no activist
lever to force one.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing:** whether the fall in
returns and margins is *cyclical* (the automotive/German R&D budget cut, which the Q1 2026
organic turn suggests is bottoming) or *structural* (generative AI deflating the bill-rates and
headcount that the whole engineering-services labour-arbitrage model rests on). If cyclical,
today's cash-flow multiple is a clear mispricing on a franchise that has compounded for a
decade. If structural, the cheapness is a low multiple on a slowly melting base — a value trap.

**Economic moat:** NARROW. The moat is real but not wide — it rests on scale (the largest
engineering-services network in Europe), long-standing client relationships and accredited
domain expertise in safety-critical engineering, which are harder to displace than commodity
IT staff-augmentation. But switching costs are modest, the work is cyclical, and pricing power

the up-cycle to roughly 6.6% now, and operating margin has compressed three years running; on

overhang on the labour-hours engineering-services model, and it is part of why the whole cohort
(Alten, Capgemini, Sopra Steria, Bertrandt) has de-rated together. But Alten's work skews toward
higher-value, regulated, safety-critical engineering that is more AI-augmented than AI-displaced,

impairment. The cheapness is therefore more fear-print than value trap — but the margin of
safety must respect that this is a shared-factor, sector-wide de-rating, not idiosyncratic alpha.

*Prepared for the investment committee. No earnings-call transcript was bundled for this
name (Alten is a French issuer that reports revenue quarterly and full accounts twice a
year), so the "management's words" layer is built from the company's own FY2025 results
release and presentation (published February 2026), the Q1 2026 revenue release (April
2026), and management commentary reported around both — all cross-checked against the hard
financials from our data provider. Where a claim rests only on management's framing rather
than an audited number, it is flagged as such.*

Alten is the largest listed engineering and research-and-development (R&D) outsourcing firm
in Europe — an "engineering services" business that rents out roughly 50,000 engineers to
design and test products for carmakers, aerospace and defence primes, rail, energy, life
sciences, telecoms and banks. It is not a diversified IT-services generalist; its economics
swing on the external R&D budgets of a handful of hardware industries, above all automotive
and aerospace. The founder, Simon Azoulay, still controls the company (roughly 57% of the
shares and a larger share of the votes) as chairman, with Cyril Malarge as chief executive.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story has moved through three distinct chapters in five years. **Chapter one (2020–2022)
was a boom.** Revenue leapt from €2.33 billion in 2020 to €3.78 billion in 2022 (+62% over
two years) as post-pandemic R&D budgets snapped back and Alten bolted on acquisitions;
reported earnings per share spiked to €13.21 in 2022, flattered by a one-off tax benefit.
Management's language in that window was pure offence — headcount growth, new-country
expansion, "structural" demand for outsourced engineering.

**Chapter two (2023–2025) was a plateau that turned into a squeeze.** Revenue stalled in a
narrow €4.07–4.14 billion band for three straight years, and by 2025 it actually shrank —
down 1.1% as reported and down 4.5% on an organic basis (stripping out acquisitions and
currency). The margin story quietly deflated in parallel: the operating margin on ordinary
activity, which had run near 11–12% at the 2022 peak, fell to 8.5% in 2025. Reported net
income collapsed from €233 million in 2023 to €107 million in 2025, and diluted earnings per
share fell from €6.74 to €3.03. The growth drivers management had emphasised — automotive and
German industrial R&D — became the drag, and the narrative shifted defensively to "utilisation
discipline", "cost control" and "limited visibility".

**Chapter three (late 2025 into 2026) is a tentative turn.** In the FY2025 release management
flagged that the slowdown *decelerated* in the fourth quarter, with civil aeronautics and
banking returning to growth and energy and defence accelerating. The Q1 2026 revenue print
then showed organic growth swing back to +1.6% (the reported figure was −0.8%, dragged down by
a weaker dollar and acquisition-integration noise). Management's framing is now cautiously
constructive — "stabilisation and growth" for 2026, a stated ambition to rebuild the operating
margin back toward 10% and grow past 70,000 engineers over time — but they are candid that
"visibility remains limited" and that the first half of 2026 is the test of whether the
recovery is real. The arc, in short: boom, to squeeze, to an unconfirmed inflection.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim / framing | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Cash generation stays robust" (FY2025 release) | Free cash flow €320m in 2025 after €416m in 2024 and €220m in 2023; free-cash-flow yield ~17%; net cash position (€59m including leases, ~€281m excluding them) | **Verified.** This is the strongest, most defensible part of the story — the business converts profit to cash and carries no net financial debt. |
| Operating margin "above the anticipated level" (8.5% vs ~8.1% expected) | Operating profit on activity €346.5m on €4,099m revenue = 8.5% | **Verified.** Management delivered slightly above the modest bar it set — a genuine, if small, credibility mark. |
| Demand is "stabilising", Q4 slowdown decelerating, Q1 2026 organic +1.6% | Organic revenue: −4.5% for FY2025 turning to +1.6% in Q1 2026 | **Verified but early.** The inflection is real in the reported organic figure, but one quarter after a full year of contraction is not yet a trend, and automotive/Germany is still shrinking. |

The central forensic point: **on reported earnings Alten looks expensive (about 17 times
depressed 2025 net income), but on cash flow it is strikingly cheap** (enterprise value —
market value plus debt minus cash — of about 4.4 times earnings before interest, tax,
depreciation and amortisation, and 5.6 times free cash flow, with net cash on the balance
sheet). The gap between the two is the whole debate: is 2025 a cyclical trough of a
cash-generative franchise, or the first leg down of a structurally shrinking base?

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: turning (from declining).** Through 2023–2025 the tone shifted unmistakably from
offensive to defensive — from "structural growth" and expansion to "utilisation", "cost
discipline" and "reduced visibility", matching a business whose organic revenue was sliding.
The FY2025 and Q1 2026 communications mark the first genuine change in that register: management
volunteered that the deceleration is easing and that specific end-markets (civil aerospace,
banking, energy, defence) have turned up, while being careful *not* to over-promise — they
explicitly withheld precise 2026 margin guidance and called out that the first half is the
proof point. That combination — more constructive but deliberately unguided — reads as honest
rather than promotional.

**Reliability: Medium-to-High.** The single cleanest test available — management "anticipated"
roughly an 8.1% operating margin for 2025 and delivered 8.5% — was a modest beat, not a miss.

market has learned to discount the "return to 10% margin, 70,000 engineers" ambition until it
shows up in the printed numbers. There is no evidence of sandbagging or of aggressive
accounting; the credibility gap is about cyclical forecasting, not integrity.

depth and duration of the automotive/German weakness** — the one region and end-market
management keeps having to explain away; (2) **whether generative AI structurally deflates
engineering bill-rates and headcount** — the question hanging over every engineering- and
IT-services name in Europe, which management addresses only obliquely (positioning AI as a
productivity tool and a new service line rather than a threat to the labour-hours business
model); and (3) **margin trajectory** — management's refusal to put a dated number on the
10% ambition is exactly the point analysts push on, because the margin is the swing factor
between the cheap-cash-flow bull case and the value-trap bear case.

recession, driven by the automotive and German industrial R&D pullback.

reasonable cost of capital — meaning that *at the trough* the business is not currently earning
its keep; whether that reverts is the entire thesis.

legacy of the acquisition-led growth era and a future impairment risk if the downturn deepens.

inflecting up — the first datapoint consistent with a cyclical trough.
🟢 Management delivered slightly above its own margin bar in 2025 and communicates candidly.
🟢 Founder-owner (Azoulay, ~57%) with heavy personal stake aligned to long-run value.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

Two subtle shifts matter. First, **the end-market mix is rotating under the surface**: aerospace,
defence and energy (structurally supported by rearmament and the energy transition) are taking
share of Alten's book from automotive (structurally pressured). That improves the *quality* of
the revenue base even while the headline stalls, and it is why the organic figure inflected
before the automotive market did. Second, **the founder-control structure is the defining
governance fact and it cuts both ways** — it aligns the controlling shareholder with long-term
value and has kept the balance sheet conservative, but it also means an outside activist cannot
force a buyback, break-up or sale, and a takeover is effectively off the table. Any re-rating
here has to come from operational recovery, not from corporate action. The CEO title has passed
from Azoulay to Cyril Malarge, a normal succession rather than a strategic pivot.

**Classification: PIVOTING (turning).** Alten is a high-quality, cash-generative, net-cash
engineering franchise that has just been through a genuine cyclical squeeze in its two biggest
end-markets and is showing the first tentative signs of troughing. Capital allocation is
conservative and shareholder-aligned (steady dividend, bolt-on acquisitions, no financial
leverage), if unexciting — there is no large buyback and, given founder control, no activist
lever to force one.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing:** whether the fall in
returns and margins is *cyclical* (the automotive/German R&D budget cut, which the Q1 2026
organic turn suggests is bottoming) or *structural* (generative AI deflating the bill-rates and
headcount that the whole engineering-services labour-arbitrage model rests on). If cyclical,
today's cash-flow multiple is a clear mispricing on a franchise that has compounded for a
decade. If structural, the cheapness is a low multiple on a slowly melting base — a value trap.

**Economic moat:** NARROW. The moat is real but not wide — it rests on scale (the largest
engineering-services network in Europe), long-standing client relationships and accredited

safety must respect that this is a shared-factor, sector-wide de-rating, not idiosyncratic alpha.

**Chapter three (late 2025 into 2026) is a tentative turn.** In the FY2025 release management
flagged that the slowdown *decelerated* in the fourth quarter, with civil aeronautics and
banking returning to growth and energy and defence accelerating. The Q1 2026 revenue print
then showed organic growth swing back to +1.6% (the reported figure was −0.8%, dragged down by
a weaker dollar and acquisition-integration noise). Management's framing is now cautiously
constructive — "stabilisation and growth" for 2026, a stated ambition to rebuild the operating
margin back toward 10% and grow past 70,000 engineers over time — but they are candid that
"visibility remains limited" and that the first half of 2026 is the test of whether the
recovery is real. The arc, in short: boom, to squeeze, to an unconfirmed inflection.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim / framing | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Cash generation stays robust" (FY2025 release) | Free cash flow €320m in 2025 after €416m in 2024 and €220m in 2023; free-cash-flow yield ~17%; net cash position (€59m including leases, ~€281m excluding them) | **Verified.** This is the strongest, most defensible part of the story — the business converts profit to cash and carries no net financial debt. |
| Operating margin "above the anticipated level" (8.5% vs ~8.1% expected) | Operating profit on activity €346.5m on €4,099m revenue = 8.5% | **Verified.** Management delivered slightly above the modest bar it set — a genuine, if small, credibility mark. |
| Demand is "stabilising", Q4 slowdown decelerating, Q1 2026 organic +1.6% | Organic revenue: −4.5% for FY2025 turning to +1.6% in Q1 2026 | **Verified but early.** The inflection is real in the reported organic figure, but one quarter after a full year of contraction is not yet a trend, and automotive/Germany is still shrinking. |
| Ambition to "restore operating margin to ~10%" and grow to 70,000+ engineers | Margin has fallen three years running to 8.5%; headcount ~56,000 and roughly flat | **Aspirational, not yet evidenced.** No dated guidance attached; this is a target, not a commitment, and the numbers are still moving the other way on headcount. |
| Reported net income (€107m, EPS €3.03) as the measure of earnings power | Operating profit was €313–346m; net income was crushed by ~€118m of non-operating charges plus a high ~45% tax rate | **The story is poorer than cash reality but the headline EPS understates it.** Trough net income is depressed by non-cash and one-off items; normalised earnings power is closer to €6–7 per share, which is why the cash-flow multiples look far cheaper than the price-to-earnings ratio. |

The central forensic point: **on reported earnings Alten looks expensive (about 17 times
depressed 2025 net income), but on cash flow it is strikingly cheap** (enterprise value —
market value plus debt minus cash — of about 4.4 times earnings before interest, tax,
depreciation and amortisation, and 5.6 times free cash flow, with net cash on the balance
sheet). The gap between the two is the whole debate: is 2025 a cyclical trough of a
cash-generative franchise, or the first leg down of a structurally shrinking base?

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: turning (from declining).** Through 2023–2025 the tone shifted unmistakably from
offensive to defensive — from "structural growth" and expansion to "utilisation", "cost
discipline" and "reduced visibility", matching a business whose organic revenue was sliding.
The FY2025 and Q1 2026 communications mark the first genuine change in that register: management
volunteered that the deceleration is easing and that specific end-markets (civil aerospace,
banking, energy, defence) have turned up, while being careful *not* to over-promise — they
explicitly withheld precise 2026 margin guidance and called out that the first half is the
proof point. That combination — more constructive but deliberately unguided — reads as honest
rather than promotional.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: Medium-to-High.** The single cleanest test available — management "anticipated"
roughly an 8.1% operating margin for 2025 and delivered 8.5% — was a modest beat, not a miss.
The company has also historically converted its engineering revenue into cash reliably, which
is the hardest thing to fake. Against that, the multi-year record is one of a business that
serially disappointed on *growth* as the automotive/German R&D cycle rolled over, so the
market has learned to discount the "return to 10% margin, 70,000 engineers" ambition until it
shows up in the printed numbers. There is no evidence of sandbagging or of aggressive
accounting; the credibility gap is about cyclical forecasting, not integrity.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The recurring pressure points, evident in how management frames each release, are: (1) **the
depth and duration of the automotive/German weakness** — the one region and end-market
management keeps having to explain away; (2) **whether generative AI structurally deflates
engineering bill-rates and headcount** — the question hanging over every engineering- and
IT-services name in Europe, which management addresses only obliquely (positioning AI as a
productivity tool and a new service line rather than a threat to the labour-hours business
model); and (3) **margin trajectory** — management's refusal to put a dated number on the
10% ambition is exactly the point analysts push on, because the margin is the swing factor
between the cheap-cash-flow bull case and the value-trap bear case.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 Organic revenue turned negative in 2025 (−4.5%), the first real contraction outside a
recession, driven by the automotive and German industrial R&D pullback.
🔴 Return on invested capital has fallen to roughly 6.6% on a trailing basis — below a
reasonable cost of capital — meaning that *at the trough* the business is not currently earning
its keep; whether that reverts is the entire thesis.
🔴 Operating margin has declined three years running (from ~11–12% to 8.5%).
🔴 Goodwill of about €1.24 billion sits on the balance sheet (down from €1.39 billion), a
legacy of the acquisition-led growth era and a future impairment risk if the downturn deepens.
🟢 Net cash balance sheet (cash €348m against €67m of financial debt excluding leases) and a
~17% free-cash-flow yield — genuine downside protection and optionality.
🟢 Q1 2026 organic growth back to +1.6%, with civil aerospace, defence, energy and banking
inflecting up — the first datapoint consistent with a cyclical trough.
🟢 Management delivered slightly above its own margin bar in 2025 and communicates candidly.
🟢 Founder-owner (Azoulay, ~57%) with heavy personal stake aligned to long-run value.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

Two subtle shifts matter. First, **the end-market mix is rotating under the surface**: aerospace,
defence and energy (structurally supported by rearmament and the energy transition) are taking
share of Alten's book from automotive (structurally pressured). That improves the *quality* of
the revenue base even while the headline stalls, and it is why the organic figure inflected
before the automotive market did. Second, **the founder-control structure is the defining
governance fact and it cuts both ways** — it aligns the controlling shareholder with long-term
value and has kept the balance sheet conservative, but it also means an outside activist cannot
force a buyback, break-up or sale, and a takeover is effectively off the table. Any re-rating
here has to come from operational recovery, not from corporate action. The CEO title has passed
from Azoulay to Cyril Malarge, a normal succession rather than a strategic pivot.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING (turning).** Alten is a high-quality, cash-generative, net-cash
engineering franchise that has just been through a genuine cyclical squeeze in its two biggest
end-markets and is showing the first tentative signs of troughing. Capital allocation is
conservative and shareholder-aligned (steady dividend, bolt-on acquisitions, no financial
leverage), if unexciting — there is no large buyback and, given founder control, no activist
lever to force one.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing:** whether the fall in
returns and margins is *cyclical* (the automotive/German R&D budget cut, which the Q1 2026
organic turn suggests is bottoming) or *structural* (generative AI deflating the bill-rates and
headcount that the whole engineering-services labour-arbitrage model rests on). If cyclical,
today's cash-flow multiple is a clear mispricing on a franchise that has compounded for a
decade. If structural, the cheapness is a low multiple on a slowly melting base — a value trap.

**Economic moat:** NARROW. The moat is real but not wide — it rests on scale (the largest
engineering-services network in Europe), long-standing client relationships and accredited
domain expertise in safety-critical engineering, which are harder to displace than commodity
IT staff-augmentation. But switching costs are modest, the work is cyclical, and pricing power
is limited. **Moat trend: ERODING** — return on invested capital has fallen from mid-teens in
the up-cycle to roughly 6.6% now, and operating margin has compressed three years running; on
the evidence, the durable earnings base is narrowing, not widening, even if part of that is
cyclical. **Secular threat: material (not terminal).** Generative AI is a genuine, unresolved
overhang on the labour-hours engineering-services model, and it is part of why the whole cohort
(Alten, Capgemini, Sopra Steria, Bertrandt) has de-rated together. But Alten's work skews toward
higher-value, regulated, safety-critical engineering that is more AI-augmented than AI-displaced,
so the threat is best read as margin/mix pressure over years, not an imminent terminal
impairment. The cheapness is therefore more fear-print than value trap — but the margin of
safety must respect that this is a shared-factor, sector-wide de-rating, not idiosyncratic alpha.
